useCases.title: Delegated access (consent only)
useCases.oneLiner: The user consented, and the act claim proves the agent acted on their behalf — fully attributable.
useCases.buyerStory: Every agent action must trace back to a real human's consent — no anonymous agent access.
useCases.pingOneSolution: After the user consents, RFC 8693 token exchange mints a delegated token carrying act={agent}; the gateway and Authorize verify the chain.
useCases.whatLong: An AI agent calls a financial tool on the user's behalf after consent. This consent-only scenario shows the complete RFC 8693 token-exchange chain: user token → delegated agent token carrying act={agent} → gateway validation → Authorize decision → tool. It does not add a transaction MFA gate.
useCases.businessValue: Every agent action is cryptographically tied to the user who authorized it. Audit teams get a full chain of custody from user login to tool call — no hand-rolled attribution, no guesswork.

productRoles.idp: Authenticates the user and mints the delegated token via RFC 8693 exchange, embedding the act claim.
productRoles.gw: Validates the token (aud, exp, act) and routes the call only after a PERMIT decision.
productRoles.authz: Evaluates the act claim and delegation chain; returns PERMIT for a valid actor.

useCases.explicitTitle: Delegated access: consent mints an agent token that acts for you
useCases.valueStatement: You approve once; your agent can then act for you, and every action traces back to your consent — no shared password, no anonymous access.

useCases.title: A2A delegation
useCases.oneLiner: Generalist hands off to specialist — the nested act claim shows the full chain back to the user.
useCases.buyerStory: A generalist agent handing off to a specialist must carry proof of the original user's authorization through the entire chain.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne mints a nested-act delegated token for the specialist; scope is narrowed at each hop.
useCases.whatLong: A generalist AI agent hands a task to a specialist sub-agent. Without enforced delegation chains, the specialist acts with the original user's full authority — no narrowing, no proof of the handoff. This scenario demonstrates nested-act token exchange so each hop is attributable and scoped.
useCases.businessValue: Multi-agent pipelines stay governed end-to-end. Each specialist inherits only the scope the handoff explicitly granted — least privilege across agent hops, with the full chain visible in the token.

productRoles.idp: Mints a nested-act delegated token for the specialist, narrowing scope at each exchange hop.
productRoles.gw: Validates the nested act chain on the A2A gateway audience and routes the specialist tool call after PERMIT.
productRoles.authz: Evaluates the full act chain at each hop; denies if any link is unauthorized.

useCases.explicitTitle: A2A delegation: your generalist agent hands a task to a specialist agent
useCases.valueStatement: Multi-agent work stays governed end-to-end: each specialist inherits only the scope the handoff granted, so adding agents never widens access.

useCases.title: A2A Orchestrator — Interactive Learning
useCases.oneLiner: Generalist asks an orchestrator to find the right specialist — the nested act chain proves the full handoff.
useCases.buyerStory: See how a generalist AI agent detects and routes tasks to specialist sub-agents using multi-agent orchestration and RFC 8693 delegation.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne + multi-agent CrewAI orchestrator analyzes requests, selects specialist agents, and chains delegated tokens with narrowed scopes.
useCases.whatLong: A generalist AI agent receives a complex request and determines it should delegate to a specialist sub-agent. The orchestrator (CrewAI with heuristic fallback) analyzes the message, identifies the best specialist, and orchestrates a two-hop delegation: generalist → specialist with a narrowed RFC 8693 nested-act token. Each hop is attributable and scoped. Watch the token chain and activity panel as the orchestration unfolds in real time.
useCases.businessValue: Multi-agent pipelines become self-organizing. Agents detect when tasks are out of their expertise and route to specialists without hard-coded task mapping. Each hop is governed end-to-end with proven scope narrowing and full auditability — no manual agent orchestration config needed.

productRoles.idp: Mints nested-act delegated tokens for each hop; generalist token → specialist token with narrowed scopes.
productRoles.gw: Routes each leg of the orchestration; the token chain proves who acted for whom.
productRoles.authz: Evaluates the full act chain at each hop and narrows policy context for the specialist.

useCases.explicitTitle: A2A orchestrator: how the right specialist is found and the handoff proven
useCases.valueStatement: You can see the full delegation chain before trusting an automated handoff — the proof is in the token, not a promise.

useCases.title: A2A end to end — protocol + identity
useCases.oneLiner: Two things are called A2A. Here they are side by side, with the real Agent Card, a real 401 when the bearer is missing, and a real nested-act chain.
useCases.buyerStory: Show a buyer what "agent-to-agent" actually means on the wire and in the token, with the real artifacts rather than a diagram.
useCases.pingOneSolution: One page carries both halves: PingOne mints the nested-act RFC 8693 chain, and the Linux Foundation A2A wire protocol discovers the specialist by Agent Card and calls it with its own PingOne bearer.
useCases.whatLong: A walkthrough of A2A using this demo's own agent. Signed out it still teaches with live artifacts: the Agent Card is fetched unauthenticated from the browser, and a JSON-RPC call sent with no Authorization header returns the real 401 that proves the wire hop is gated. Signed in, "Run the delegation" executes the real chain and the page renders every hop: two client_credentials tokens, two RFC 8693 exchanges, the scope narrowing, and the act nesting Authorize decides over. Each pane states what its data actually is — a reconstructed parameter summary, decoded claims, or a genuine HTTP request — because the evidence is real but it is not a captured HTTP transcript.
useCases.businessValue: Removes the most common confusion in agent-to-agent conversations: the wire protocol and the identity chain are different layers with different credentials. Seeing the Agent Card, the refusal, and the nested act claim in one place turns an architecture debate into a five-minute demo.

productRoles.idp: Mints both the nested-act delegated token and the separate client_credentials bearer the wire hop authenticates with.
productRoles.gw: Serves the public Agent Card and enforces the bearer requirement on the JSON-RPC endpoint.
productRoles.authz: Decides over the full act chain — ActChainDepth 2, specialist acting for generalist acting for the user.

useCases.explicitTitle: A2A end to end: the agent protocol (Agent Card, 401) and the identity chain side by side
useCases.valueStatement: One demo shows both halves of agent-to-agent: the wire protocol AND the identity — so 'A2A' never hides an ungoverned shortcut.

useCases.title: A2A generalist mismatch
useCases.oneLiner: Same user, same delegation shape — but an unregistered agent identity is denied. Authorization keys on WHO is acting, not just who they act for.
useCases.buyerStory: A resource server must be able to tell WHICH agent is acting on the user's behalf, not just that some agent is — the same user with a different, unregistered agent must be denied.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne Authorize evaluates the nested act chain's actor identity, not just the subject — an unregistered generalist is denied even though the user and the delegation shape are otherwise valid.
useCases.whatLong: Runs the same real, governed delegation as A2A delegation (a genuine PERMIT), then probes the same PingOne Authorize decision the gateway calls with a fabricated, unregistered actor identity in place of the real generalist. The result is a genuine invalid_a2a_generalist DENY from live policy — proof that authorization decisions account for the AGENT's identity, not only the user's. The probe does not mint a real second agent token; it demonstrates the policy branch directly.
useCases.businessValue: A stolen or rogue agent credential cannot ride on a legitimate user's delegation shape — the policy engine denies based on actor identity even when the subject and act-chain depth look correct. This is the authorization half of the delegation-chain value proposition (the audit-trail half is UC2/UC2.5).

productRoles.idp: Mints the real leg-1 delegated token exactly as UC2; the mismatch probe itself mints no token.
productRoles.gw: Not involved in the probe leg — the probe calls the decision endpoint directly, same contract the gateway uses.
productRoles.authz: Evaluates ActChainDepth and NestedActClientId; DENYs invalid_a2a_generalist when the actor does not match the registered generalist.

useCases.explicitTitle: A2A security: an unregistered specialist agent is refused
useCases.valueStatement: Only agents your organization registered can act for you — a rogue agent can't slip into a delegation chain by knowing the endpoint.

useCases.title: act gate
useCases.oneLiner: The actor token identifies the agent; PingOne Authorize checks the user's consent (may_act) on every call — revoke and the next call is denied, without waiting for the delegated token to expire.
useCases.buyerStory: An agent should only be allowed to act on a user's behalf if that user explicitly authorized it.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne mints the exchanged token's act claim from the actor token — the agent is identified at exchange time; the authorization server then checks the user's consent (may_act) on EVERY tool call: no matching consent, no permit. Revoking the user's agent authorization takes effect without waiting for the delegated token to expire (the revoke forces a silent re-auth, which refreshes the bridged consent). (Legacy mode seeds act from may_act at mint instead — ff_may_act_seed.)
useCases.whatLong: Token exchange mints the act claim from the actor token — the agent identifies itself by its own credential, not by a user-side seed. Consent is enforced per call: the user's may_act authorization is bridged to PingOne Authorize on every tool call, and a call whose acting agent doesn't match is denied. Revoking the user's agent authorization takes effect at the next silent re-auth (which the revoke triggers) — without waiting for the delegated token's expiry window. (Legacy mode: ff_may_act_seed ON seeds act from may_act at mint time, the pre-2026-10 behavior.)
useCases.businessValue: Users control which agents can act for them. The gate is enforced at the authorization server on every call (not just at token mint) — no per-app code required — so adding or revoking agent authorization is a config change, not a deployment.

productRoles.idp: Mints the act claim from the actor token during exchange (default); may_act seeding behind ff_may_act_seed.
productRoles.authz: Checks the user's bridged consent (may_act) against the acting agent on every tool call — no match, no permit.

useCases.explicitTitle: act gate: every agent action names its actor and its human
useCases.valueStatement: Nothing an agent does is anonymous: security teams can always answer 'who did this, through which agent, for which user'.

useCases.title: Non-human (agent) identity lifecycle
useCases.oneLiner: This is the live agent identity, so the exchange succeeds. Retire or rotate that agent app in the PingOne console and run it again — the same call dies at the exchange step, with no per-tool cleanup anywhere.
useCases.buyerStory: Calls from a retired or orphaned agent identity should fail — agent identities need a full lifecycle just like human ones.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne manages the agent app as a first-class identity; rotating or retiring the client credential blocks all subsequent calls.
useCases.whatLong: A retired or orphaned agent application still holds credentials. Without lifecycle management, those credentials remain valid indefinitely. This scenario demonstrates what happens when the agent app's client credential is revoked in PingOne — subsequent token exchange requests fail, cutting off all tool access immediately.
useCases.businessValue: Agent identities are managed with the same lifecycle rigor as human identities. Retiring a credential in PingOne is instant and complete — no per-tool, per-API, or per-service cleanup required.

productRoles.idp: Manages the agent app as a first-class identity; disabling or rotating the credential blocks all subsequent token exchanges.

useCases.explicitTitle: Agent identity lifecycle: register, rotate and revoke agent keys like employee badges
useCases.valueStatement: Agents are managed like employees: joiners get keys, movers get rotations, leavers get cut off — one process your IAM team already runs.

useCases.title: Agent observability and traceability
useCases.oneLiner: Every step is logged with useCaseId and the act chain — the full trace is always reconstructable.
useCases.buyerStory: Every agent action must be attributable end-to-end — who the agent was, who it acted for, and what it did.
useCases.pingOneSolution: Every token event and activity log is stamped with useCaseId and the act chain; both evidence panels reconstruct the full trace.
useCases.whatLong: After every agent action, there must be a complete, reconstructable audit trail: who the agent was, who authorized it, what it did, and what the policy decided. This scenario demonstrates the full trace — from user login through token exchange, Authorize decision, and tool dispatch — surfaced in the evidence panels.
useCases.businessValue: Compliance and incident response depend on traceable agent actions. The useCaseId, act chain, and decision outcome are stamped on every event — building a complete, immutable audit trail without any application-layer instrumentation.

productRoles.idp: Stamps the act chain on every token event; the exchange history is the attribution record.
productRoles.gw: Logs the tool call, the acting agent, and the Authorize decision outcome.
productRoles.authz: Records the policy decision (PERMIT/DENY/STEP_UP) for every evaluated request.

useCases.explicitTitle: Agent observability: every action traceable end to end
useCases.valueStatement: When something goes wrong you have the full story in minutes, not a forensics project: every hop, every decision, attributable.

useCases.title: My mortgage
useCases.oneLiner: Same delegated token, a different tool — the act claim proves the agent all the way to a mortgage lookup, not just a balance check.
useCases.buyerStory: Delegated-access proof can't be special-cased per tool — every account type the agent touches needs the same chain of custody, not just the everyday balance check.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The same RFC 8693 delegated token (act={agent}) authorizes every tool call, including less-common products like a mortgage — one token exchange covers the whole tool surface.
useCases.whatLong: Delegated-access proof isn't special-cased per tool. This scenario runs the identical RFC 8693 chain from UC1 — user token, act={agent}, gateway validation, Authorize decision — against a less-common tool (mortgage lookup) to show the proof travels with every call the agent makes, not just the common ones.
useCases.businessValue: Attribution coverage doesn't shrink as the agent's tool surface grows. Adding a new tool never means adding new attribution plumbing — every call already carries the same proof.

productRoles.idp: Mints the same delegated token regardless of which tool the agent calls next.
productRoles.gw: Validates the token identically no matter which tool it is routed to.
productRoles.authz: Evaluates the same act-claim policy for every tool in scope.

useCases.explicitTitle: My mortgage: your agent working on a real customer journey end to end
useCases.valueStatement: This isn't a toy flow: the same governance that guards a demo mortgage guards your production customer journeys.

useCases.title: Spot unusual patterns
useCases.oneLiner: The analysis path runs the full pipeline — same RFC 8693 → gateway → Authorize legs as a heuristic chip, no shortcut.
useCases.buyerStory: A security-aware agent should be able to reason over live activity, not just execute fixed lookups — and that reasoning has to run through the same governed pipeline as everything else.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The free-form LLM path runs through the identical RFC 8693 → gateway → Authorize legs as a heuristic chip — reasoning is not a shortcut around the policy chain.
useCases.whatLong: Not every useful agent action is a fixed lookup. This scenario asks the agent to reason freely over recent activity for anything unusual — the LLM decides what to look at and how to summarize it, but every underlying tool call it makes still goes through the same token-exchange and Authorize legs as a deterministic chip.
useCases.businessValue: Free-form reasoning does not create a policy gap. Whatever the agent decides to look at, every tool call it actually makes is still attributed and authorized — reasoning changes what runs, never whether it is governed.

productRoles.gw: Validates and routes every tool call the reasoning step issues, same as any other call.
productRoles.authz: Evaluates each resulting tool call independently — freeform intent grants no special access.

useCases.explicitTitle: Anomaly detection: unusual patterns surface before damage
useCases.valueStatement: Odd agent behavior — new payees, odd hours, velocity — is caught and checked, not silently executed.

useCases.title: Why was that blocked?
useCases.oneLiner: The agent explained its own security posture from the live token-chain events — useful for teaching why a control fired.
useCases.buyerStory: When a control fires, the person watching the demo should be able to ask the agent to explain itself in plain language — backed by the real evidence, not a canned line.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The agent explains its own security posture by reading the live token-chain events, not a scripted explanation — the explanation is only as good as the evidence PingOne actually produced.
useCases.whatLong: After a control fires (a DENY, a step-up, a consent gate), the agent can be asked to explain what just happened. It reads the real token-chain events from the run — not a canned script — and narrates the decision in plain language, teaching the audience why the control triggered.
useCases.businessValue: Every enforcement decision is self-explaining. Support and audit teams get a plain-language narration of what PingOne decided and why, sourced from the same evidence an auditor would pull, not a separate explanation system that can drift from reality.

productRoles.authz: Recorded the original PERMIT/DENY/STEP_UP decision the explanation is built from.

useCases.explicitTitle: Explainable denial: exactly why an agent action was blocked
useCases.valueStatement: When something is blocked you get the reason in plain language — support can resolve tickets without a forensic dig.

useCases.title: Overscoped agent
useCases.oneLiner: The agent asked for write when it only needed read — least-privilege narrows it before any tool runs.
useCases.buyerStory: An agent holding more scope than the task needs is a standing privilege-escalation risk.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The scope topology surfaces the mismatch; least-privilege hygiene narrows the token to only what the tool requires.
useCases.whatLong: An agent requests broader OAuth scopes than the task actually needs — for example, write scope to perform a read-only operation. This creates a standing privilege that can be exploited if the token is stolen or the agent misbehaves. The scenario surfaces the mismatch using the scope topology.
useCases.businessValue: Least-privilege enforcement catches scope bloat before it becomes a risk. Security teams can audit every agent's effective scope against what the tools actually require — with a single canonical topology file as the source of truth.

productRoles.idp: Issues the token with the scopes the agent requested; the topology then surfaces any excess.
productRoles.gw: Enforces the required scopes at the gateway boundary — excess scope is harmless here but the mismatch is visible.
productRoles.authz: Evaluates scope requirements per tool; a token carrying only the needed scope is the correct posture.

useCases.explicitTitle: Overscoped agent: the agent asks for write, the mint grants only read
useCases.valueStatement: Least privilege at mint time: even a misconfigured or compromised agent gets the minimum scope for the task, not what it asked for.

useCases.title: Authz denied
useCases.oneLiner: $2500 exceeds the policy ceiling — Authorize returns DENY before the transfer runs.
useCases.buyerStory: A policy-violating agent action — like an amount over the limit — must be denied before the tool executes.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne Authorize evaluates the request and returns DENY; the gateway stops the call.
useCases.whatLong: An agent attempts a transaction that exceeds a hard policy ceiling — for example, a $2,500 transfer. The Authorize engine evaluates the request before the tool runs and returns DENY. The gateway stops the call; no money moves.
useCases.businessValue: Policy enforcement is externalized and instant. Changing the deny ceiling is a rule edit — not a code change — and takes effect immediately across every agent and every channel.

productRoles.idp: Issues the delegated token the agent presents at the gateway.
productRoles.gw: Forwards the request to Authorize; stops the tool call on DENY.
productRoles.authz: Evaluates the transaction amount against the ceiling rule and returns DENY.

useCases.explicitTitle: Authorization denied: an unregistered agent is refused at the gateway
useCases.valueStatement: Only allow-listed agents reach your data: an attacker's agent is refused before any tool runs, whatever token it presents.

useCases.title: MFA step-up (HITL)
useCases.oneLiner: $600 >= $500 → MFA required, then it proceeds.
useCases.buyerStory: A high-value agent action shouldn't go through on the agent's say-so alone; a human must complete MFA.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne Authorize returns a step-up obligation; the human-in-the-loop completes MFA before PERMIT.
useCases.whatLong: An agent attempts a mid-range transfer ($600). The amount clears the step-up threshold but not the hard deny ceiling. Authorize returns a step-up obligation — the agent must pause, the user must satisfy MFA, and only then does the policy re-evaluate to PERMIT.
useCases.businessValue: High-value actions get a proportional gate. Step-up is policy-driven, not hard-coded: the threshold is a rule you change in the Authorize console without redeploying anything.

productRoles.idp: Authenticates the user and mints the delegated agent token.
productRoles.gw: Receives the step-up obligation from Authorize; holds the call until the MFA receipt is presented.
productRoles.authz: Returns the STEP_UP obligation for the mid-range amount; re-evaluates to PERMIT after MFA.

useCases.explicitTitle: MFA step-up: a mid-range transfer pauses until you complete MFA
useCases.valueStatement: Large actions pause for a human check — automation can't move meaningful money without you in the loop, but small everyday tasks never bug you.

useCases.title: MFA + HITL consent
useCases.oneLiner: The agent paused and waited — the transfer only ran after you approved it.
useCases.buyerStory: Some agent actions are consequential enough to require human-in-the-loop consent with MFA.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne Authorize returns a HITL obligation; the agent pauses until the human completes MFA and a verified approval receipt is received.
useCases.whatLong: An agent attempts a transfer that requires more than a user tap — a full human-in-the-loop approval. Authorize returns a HITL obligation; the agent is forced to pause and surface a consent modal. Only after the user explicitly approves is the action retried and PERMIT returned.
useCases.businessValue: Consequential agent actions are gated on verified human consent — not inferred intent. The approval is policy-triggered and auditable, with a cryptographic receipt tying the consent to the eventual tool call.

productRoles.idp: Mints the delegated token the agent uses to call the gateway.
productRoles.gw: Receives the HITL obligation; blocks the tool until the agent presents a HITL receipt.
productRoles.authz: Returns the HITL obligation; re-evaluates to PERMIT only when HitlApproved=true is presented.

useCases.explicitTitle: HITL approval: sensitive transfers need explicit human approval, not just MFA
useCases.valueStatement: For genuinely sensitive actions, a tap is not enough: an explicit approval receipt — bound to that exact transfer — is required. An approval can't be faked with MFA, and vice versa.

useCases.title: Group / entitlement check
useCases.oneLiner: The user isn't in the required group — Authorize denies regardless of scopes.
useCases.buyerStory: An agent acting for a user who is not in the required group must be denied, regardless of the token's scopes.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne Authorize evaluates the user group membership claim and returns DENY when the user is not entitled.
useCases.whatLong: A user who is not a member of the required PingOne group attempts an action that requires that membership. The Authorize policy evaluates the group claim in the token and returns DENY — regardless of whether the token's scopes would otherwise permit the action.
useCases.businessValue: Group-based entitlement decisions are centralized in policy, not scattered across services. Adding a user to a group in PingOne immediately expands what their agent can do — no code change, no cache invalidation.

productRoles.idp: Includes the user's group membership claim in the token.
productRoles.gw: Enforces the DENY returned by Authorize before any tool is dispatched.
productRoles.authz: Evaluates the group claim against the entitlement rule; returns DENY when the user is not a member.

useCases.explicitTitle: Entitlement check: outside the required group is denied regardless of scopes
useCases.valueStatement: Access follows your job role, not your token: moving teams changes access instantly, and a stolen token inherits only the victim's entitlements.

useCases.title: Group / entitlement check — live board
useCases.oneLiner: Flip the membership, run the check, watch every decision move together — the policy decides, not the token.
useCases.buyerStory: A presenter needs to show the group gate deciding LIVE — flip a membership and watch the decision move — without signing in as a different user between runs.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The /group-policy page re-reads real PingOne directory membership for every decision: the board shows one live Authorize decision per vertical for the signed-in user, and the check panel runs the same decision for any demo user on demand.
useCases.whatLong: The companion page step to UC9's chip. On /group-policy the presenter flips the signed-in user's membership with a real PingOne directory write and watches every vertical's decision move; the Run-a-group-check panel picks any demo user (demoDelegate vs demoUser) and any vertical, and fires the same authorize decision the PEP makes — same evidence chain, one call.
useCases.businessValue: Group entitlement is not a one-off chip result: it is a live policy surface. Change the directory, and the very next decision reflects it — no code change, no cache, no re-login.

productRoles.idp: Holds the group memberships the directory read returns.
productRoles.gw: Enforces the same decision before dispatching the gated tool.
productRoles.authz: Answers every decision the board and panel display.

useCases.explicitTitle: Entitlement live flip: revoke the group and the very next call is denied
useCases.valueStatement: Offboarding is instant: remove the group and the next agent call fails — no waiting for token expiry, no stale caches, no orphaned access.

useCases.title: Entitlement-tiered capability
useCases.oneLiner: Private Banking tier gets wire tools and a higher limit; Standard tier's agent is not offered them.
useCases.buyerStory: A premium-tier user's agent should have access to higher-value tools; a standard user's agent should not even see them.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne group membership drives a per-tier tool set and amount limits; the user's tier expands what the agent may do.
useCases.whatLong: A Private Banking tier user's agent should have access to higher-value tools and limits; a Standard tier user's agent should not even be offered them. PingOne group membership drives the tier — the agent's available tool set and limits expand with the user's entitlement tier.
useCases.businessValue: Tiered entitlement is policy-driven, not hard-coded. Promoting a user to a higher tier in PingOne immediately changes what their agent can do — with no code change and no redeploy.

productRoles.idp: Includes the user's tier group membership claim in the token.
productRoles.gw: Enforces the per-tier decision from Authorize before dispatching tool calls.
productRoles.authz: Evaluates the tier claim against the entitlement rule; adjusts the permitted tool set and limits.

useCases.explicitTitle: Tiered capability: your entitlement level decides which tools exist and their limits
useCases.valueStatement: Upgrading your account upgrades your agent instantly — and downgrading just as instantly shrinks what it can do. No code changes.

useCases.title: CIBA out-of-band approval
useCases.oneLiner: Note the amount — $150, below the MFA threshold. A person doing this in-browser would sail through. But an AGENT moving money is a sensitive, agent-context action, so approval is requested out-of-band on the user's phone. CIBA is triggered by the action and the actor, not the amount.
useCases.buyerStory: An AI agent has no browser to prompt for step-up. When it performs a sensitive action, approval must be requested out-of-band on the user's own device — driven by the action and the agent context, not by a dollar amount.
useCases.pingOneSolution: Because an agent is acting (no browser redirect) on a sensitive money movement, PingOne Authorize returns a CIBA obligation. The backend calls bc-authorize and polls for the auth_req_id, proceeding only after the user approves out-of-band on their phone.
useCases.whatLong: An AI agent performs a sensitive action — moving money on the user's behalf — with no browser in which to prompt for step-up. PingOne CIBA (Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication) requests decoupled approval on the user's separate device. The trigger is the agent context plus the sensitivity of the action, NOT a dollar threshold: this demo uses a deliberately small $150 transfer to make that explicit — the same amount in-browser needs no step-up, yet the agent-initiated action still requires out-of-band approval. The agent polls for the result and proceeds only after the user approves on their phone.
useCases.businessValue: Out-of-band approval is meaningfully stronger than in-session step-up — a compromised browser (or a rogue agent) cannot self-approve. Basing the trigger on agent-context and action sensitivity, not amount, means an autonomous agent can never move money without a real human's decoupled confirmation. CIBA is natively supported by PingOne; no custom push infrastructure needed.

productRoles.idp: Receives the CIBA auth_req_id request and delivers the approval challenge to the user's device.
productRoles.gw: Holds the tool call until the agent presents the CIBA approval receipt.
productRoles.authz: Returns the CIBA obligation for the sensitive, agent-initiated action; PERMITs only after the user approves out-of-band.

useCases.explicitTitle: CIBA: approving agent actions out-of-band on your phone
useCases.valueStatement: Agents can prompt you even with no browser open: the approval lands on your phone, so automation never bypasses the human check.

useCases.title: Progressive trust demo — presenter guide
useCases.oneLiner: Five acts, one story — progressive trust from public catalog to policy deny, with full delegation visible in the Token Chain panel.
useCases.buyerStory: User-owned agents should move from public access to authenticated access, in-app step-up, out-of-band approval, and hard deny — without collapsing trust into one token.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne OAuth, Authorize, RFC 8693 token exchange, and CIBA — orchestrated by the BFF and MCP gateway while Helix, llama.cpp, or Google routes tool calls.
useCases.whatLong: Guided presenter journey mapped from the Ping Identity MyHotels blog to Super Banking. The act strip on this page references existing use cases: Act 1 (UC24 public catalog); Act 2 → UC1 delegated access; Act 3 → UC8 HITL; Act 4 → UC7 MFA step-up; optional Act 4b → UC22 CIBA when ciba_enabled; Act 5 → UC6 policy DENY. Run Act 1 from here, then Acts 2–5 on the dashboard with Token Chain and Activity panels open.
useCases.businessValue: One narrated walkthrough that shows buyers how PingOne secures user-owned agents across trust boundaries — without ChatGPT or a third-party agent host.

productRoles.idp: Authenticates the user and mints delegated tokens when protected tools are invoked.
productRoles.gw: Enforces Authorize on every tool call and performs RFC 8693 re-exchange to the MCP audience.
productRoles.authz: Returns PERMIT, HITL obligation, CIBA requirement, or DENY based on tool and transaction amount.

useCases.buyerStory: Users should explore low-risk information before signing in — auth only when value is clear.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The public catalog path skips PingOne Authorize, the Agent Gateway, and token exchange.
useCases.whatLong: Act 1 of the progressive trust demo. The agent answers a public branch-catalog question without authentication — mirroring the MyHotels public hotel search. The local public tool (get_branch_hours) does not call PingOne Authorize or the Agent Gateway.
useCases.businessValue: Demonstrates progressive authentication — users are not forced to sign in before seeing non-sensitive catalog data.

productRoles.gw: Not in path for this local public catalog request.
productRoles.authz: Not called for this public catalog request.

useCases.explicitTitle: Public catalog: browsing needs no identity, but action does
useCases.valueStatement: Anonymous visitors can browse freely while every real action stays gated — good UX and zero anonymous risk in one pattern.

useCases.title: Proof of enforcement — live verdict on every use case
useCases.oneLiner: You don't have to take the agent's word for it — watch the verdict prove it, live, for whatever you just triggered.
useCases.buyerStory: Buyers shouldn't have to trust the chat reply — every enforcement decision should be visibly, verifiably proven on screen, not just claimed.
useCases.pingOneSolution: Every tool call is tagged end-to-end with the triggering useCaseId and active vertical (chip, launcher, or attack sim; any agent mode), stamped onto the token chain, the PingOne Authorize decision, and the activity log. A client-side verdict engine compares what actually happened against each use case's declared evidence and expected outcome, then renders the result live.
useCases.whatLong: A cross-cutting capability, not a single narrative: whenever any of the use cases above fires (chip, Use-Case Launcher, or attack simulation, in Heuristics or any LLM mode), three surfaces render a verdict comparing the real trace against that use case's declared evidence — an inline strip under the chat reply, a use-case-aware checklist card in the Token Chain panel, and a room-facing "Verified" banner that expands into the full trace. States: verified, denied-as-expected (for attacks/step-up/HITL), mismatch (the real outcome contradicted what was expected — the signal this feature exists to surface), and incomplete (evidence still arriving).
useCases.businessValue: Turns "trust the demo" into "watch the proof" — every enforcement claim in every other use case on this page is independently, visibly verified rather than asserted.

productRoles.idp: PingOne Authorize's real decision is what the verdict is checked against — nothing is simulated for this capability.
productRoles.gw: Every tool call is tagged with useCaseId + vertical before dispatch, so the authorize decision and activity log carry it end to end.

useCases.explicitTitle: Proof of enforcement: every use case shows its live verdict
useCases.valueStatement: Nothing here is a slide: every claim on this dashboard is backed by a real decision you can replay — enforcement you can demonstrate to auditors.

useCases.title: Wrong / insufficient scope
useCases.oneLiner: The token had read scope, the tool needed write — scope enforcement stopped it cold.
useCases.buyerStory: An agent with the wrong scope should never reach the tool — scope enforcement is the last line of defense.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The MCP server validates required scopes before dispatching; a token missing a required scope yields DENY.
useCases.whatLong: An agent's token is missing a required scope — for example, a read-only token attempting a write tool call. Scope enforcement at the gateway is the last line of defense: the tool must never execute if the token cannot satisfy its scope requirement.
useCases.businessValue: Scope enforcement is automatic and centralized. No tool needs to re-validate scopes in application code — the gateway and MCP server enforce the topology contract before dispatch.

productRoles.idp: Issues the token with only the scopes the agent was granted.
productRoles.gw: Checks required scopes against the token before routing; returns DENY_403 on mismatch.

useCases.explicitTitle: Wrong scope: a read-scoped token calling a write tool is refused 403
useCases.valueStatement: Scope enforcement stops privilege escalation cold: a stolen or misused token can read what it may read — and nothing more.

useCases.title: Resource-ownership / account takeover
useCases.oneLiner: The agent tried to read another user's account — Authorize matched the resource owner and denied it.
useCases.buyerStory: An agent must never act on another user's resources — even with a valid token.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne Authorize binds the resource to the token subject; a cross-owner request is denied.
useCases.whatLong: An agent presents a valid delegated token but attempts to read an account belonging to a different user. The Authorize policy binds the resource to the token subject — even a valid, scoped, properly-delegated token is denied if the requested resource belongs to someone else.
useCases.businessValue: Resource-ownership checks are automatic and policy-driven. Applications do not need to implement owner checks in business logic — Authorize enforces them for every agent call, without exception.

productRoles.idp: Issues the token with the subject (user) claim that Authorize checks against the resource owner.
productRoles.gw: Stops the tool call on DENY before any data is returned.
productRoles.authz: Binds the resource to the token sub; returns DENY on an ownership mismatch.

useCases.explicitTitle: Account takeover blocked: an agent reading someone else's account is denied
useCases.valueStatement: Even a fully valid agent token can't cross customer boundaries: your agent can only see YOUR accounts, however it's phrased.

useCases.title: Bad client → agent gateway
useCases.oneLiner: Wrong audience → the gateway refuses it before a tool is ever touched.
useCases.buyerStory: A malformed or stolen token must never reach the tools.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The gateway validates aud/exp/iss/nbf before any routing; a bad token is rejected with 401.
useCases.whatLong: An agent presents a token with the wrong audience — or a malformed, expired, or incorrectly signed token. The gateway validates aud, exp, iss, and nbf before any routing occurs; the call is rejected with 401 and no tool is ever touched.
useCases.businessValue: Token validation at the gateway perimeter means that all downstream services are shielded from malformed credentials. A single enforcement point replaces per-service token checks.

productRoles.gw: Validates aud/exp/iss/nbf on every inbound token; rejects malformed tokens with 401 before routing.

useCases.explicitTitle: Wrong audience: a token minted for another API is refused 401
useCases.valueStatement: Tokens are destination-locked: a credential stolen from one system is worthless at another — the breach doesn't spread sideways.

useCases.title: Token theft / replay defense
useCases.oneLiner: With DPoP on, a stolen token is worthless without the private key: the gateway refuses a replayed proof (401 invalid_dpop_proof). Audience binding is unconditional underneath.
useCases.buyerStory: A stolen token must be unusable — audience binding and DPoP key binding ensure it can't be replayed.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The gateway binds the delegated token to a DPoP key (cnf.jkt) and refuses a reused proof — this step replays one proof and the gateway rejects the second with 401 invalid_dpop_proof. Audience binding (D-05) is enforced unconditionally underneath.
useCases.whatLong: A valid, correctly-audienced delegated token is DPoP-bound (cnf.jkt). The agent signs one proof and calls the gateway — accepted. The SAME proof is then replayed: the gateway's replay cache refuses it with 401 invalid_dpop_proof. A stolen bearer plus a captured proof is worthless — the proof works exactly once, and only from the holder of the private key. Audience binding is enforced unconditionally as a second layer.
useCases.businessValue: Two layers of replay defense with no application changes: audience binding stops a token being spent at another service, and DPoP key binding stops a stolen token being replayed at all.

productRoles.idp: Mints the token with a specific aud and binds it to the agent's DPoP key (cnf.jkt) when DPoP is on.
productRoles.gw: Enforces aud binding unconditionally; verifies the DPoP proof and refuses a reused one (jti replay cache) with 401 invalid_dpop_proof.

useCases.explicitTitle: Token theft + replay: DPoP makes a stolen bearer token worthless
useCases.valueStatement: A stolen token alone can't be used: the attacker also needs the private key on your device, and captured proofs can't be replayed.

useCases.title: Confused-deputy actor injection
useCases.oneLiner: Actor identity comes from a native, PingOne-issued claim on the token — never from a header. Headers are only a fallback for hops where PingOne can't natively stamp an actor; they can never override a real claim. That's why this rogue actor is denied.
useCases.buyerStory: A rogue agent forcing itself into the act claim must be caught — only the authorized actor is allowed.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne stamps a native, cryptographically-issued act claim on the exchanged token whenever the actor actually performed the RFC 8693 exchange. The gateway and Authorize always prefer that native claim over any header — a header can only fill in on hops where no native claim exists. A rogue actor can't win by spoofing a header; it would have to perform a real token exchange as an unauthorized client, and Authorize's ActClientId check on the resulting native claim then denies it.
useCases.whatLong: A rogue agent tries to force itself into the delegation chain by claiming to be the authorized actor. PingOne's resource attribute mapping stamps a native act claim on the exchanged token whenever a real RFC 8693 actor-token exchange happened — that claim always wins over any header. Only on hops where PingOne can't natively emit act does the gateway fall back to a trusted, internal-secret-gated header bridge. Either way, the ActClientId Authorize receives traces back to a real, authenticated exchange — never an attacker-controlled value.
useCases.businessValue: Actor identity is anchored to a real token exchange, not a request header. Even a compromised internal service that could forge headers still can't spoof identity once PingOne has stamped a native claim — there is no path for a rogue actor to talk its way past the authorized-actor check.

productRoles.gw: Prefers the token's native act claim; falls back to the trusted X-Act-Client-Id header bridge only when no native claim is present, then forwards act.sub to Authorize as ActClientId.
productRoles.authz: Checks ActClientId against the configured authorized actor; returns DENY for any other value.

useCases.explicitTitle: Confused deputy: a forged actor header can't change who the agent acts for
useCases.valueStatement: Identity travels in signed claims, not headers: an attacker can't launder their actions through a legitimate agent by editing metadata.

useCases.title: PAR + RAR intent violation (pushed intent exceeded)
useCases.oneLiner: The agent tried to transfer more than the RAR granted — Authorize caught the overage and denied it.
useCases.buyerStory: An agent that exceeds the amount or payee granted via Pushed Authorization Request (RFC 9126) must be denied.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne Authorize evaluates the PAR-submitted authorization details; exceeding the granted amount or payee yields DENY.
useCases.whatLong: An agent was authorized via a Rich Authorization Request (RFC 9396) for a specific amount and payee. It then attempts a transfer that exceeds the granted authorization_details. Authorize evaluates the RAR context and returns DENY when the actual request exceeds the intent.
useCases.businessValue: RAR ties authorization to a specific intent — amount, payee, purpose. An agent cannot exceed what the user explicitly approved, even if the token scopes would otherwise allow it.

productRoles.idp: Mints the token with the authorization_details claim encoding the approved intent.
productRoles.gw: Forwards the intent context to Authorize and enforces the DENY.
productRoles.authz: Compares the live request parameters against the RAR grant; returns DENY on overage.

useCases.explicitTitle: PAR+RAR intent exceeded: the agent tries to spend beyond what was consented
useCases.valueStatement: Pushed consent is a hard ceiling: the agent cannot spend a cent more than the exact intent you approved, even inside its normal tier.

useCases.title: PAR + RAR intent verified (PERMIT)
useCases.oneLiner: Same RAR grant UC14 attacks, but requested within the cap — the gateway and PingOne Authorize permit it and the token chain shows an Intent Verified step.
useCases.buyerStory: A transfer that stays within its PAR (RFC 9126) request_uri authorization cap is verified and permitted — the legitimate counterpart to the PAR overage attack.
useCases.pingOneSolution: RFC 9126 PAR authorization details bind the transfer to an amount cap; the MCP gateway and PingOne Authorize verify the requested transfer against it before permitting.
useCases.whatLong: A learning scenario (not an attack): the counterpart to UC14 (RAR overage attack). Here, the agent was authorized via RFC 9396 Rich Authorization Request for a specific transfer amount and payee. The agent requests a transfer that stays within the granted authorization_details. The gateway and PingOne Authorize verify the request against the RAR grant and return PERMIT — the token chain shows an Intent Verified step.
useCases.businessValue: RAR ties authorization to the exact user intent — the agent can only do what was explicitly approved. This scenario shows the happy path where the agent respects the limits.
useCases.explicitTitle: PAR+RAR intent honored: the exact consented amount permits
useCases.valueStatement: The same mechanism that blocks overreach allows exactly what you approved — consent is precise, not a blanket 'yes'.

useCases.title: Intent-token tampering
useCases.oneLiner: The intent token was altered — the signature check caught the tampering before any tool ran.
useCases.buyerStory: A tampered or expired intent token must be detected before it can authorize a larger or different action.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The gateway validates the intent token signature and expiry; a tampered or expired token is rejected.
useCases.whatLong: An intent token (encoding the approved transaction parameters) is tampered with — the amount or payee is altered before the agent presents it. The gateway validates the token signature and expiry; a tampered or expired intent token is rejected before any tool runs.
useCases.businessValue: Cryptographic signing of intent tokens means any in-flight modification is immediately detectable — even if the attacker has network access. No application code needs to verify intent integrity.

productRoles.idp: Signs the intent token at issuance, providing the cryptographic baseline for gateway validation.
productRoles.gw: Validates the intent token signature and expiry; rejects tampered or expired tokens with 401.

useCases.explicitTitle: Intent tampering: an edited consent token fails its signature check
useCases.valueStatement: Consent can't be forged after the fact: changing the approved amount invalidates the signature before the value is ever read.

useCases.title: Impersonation blocked (OBO required)
useCases.oneLiner: No act claim means no attribution — the gateway rejects pure impersonation to keep every action traceable.
useCases.buyerStory: An agent presenting a pure impersonation token — with the user as sub but no act claim — must be rejected; only on-behalf-of delegation is allowed.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The gateway requires an act claim for agent-mediated tool calls; a missing act claim is rejected before any tool runs.
useCases.whatLong: An agent presents a token where the user is listed as sub but there is no act claim — a pure impersonation posture, not an on-behalf-of delegation. The gateway requires an act claim for all agent-mediated tool calls; a missing act claim is rejected before any tool runs.
useCases.businessValue: Every agent action must be attributable. Requiring an act claim enforces the on-behalf-of model — preventing silent impersonation and ensuring every tool call carries a verifiable chain of custody.

productRoles.gw: Requires an act claim on every agent-mediated tool call; rejects tokens without one.
productRoles.authz: Validates the act chain when present; this scenario demonstrates the absence case.

useCases.explicitTitle: Impersonation blocked: a user token with no act claim is refused
useCases.valueStatement: Every agent action is attributable: an attacker can't pretend to be you directly — the missing actor claim gives them away.

useCases.title: Raw user-token forwarding blocked (Zero Trust)
useCases.oneLiner: The agent tried to hand MCP the user's own token — the BFF refused to forward it. Only exchanged, agent-scoped tokens with an act claim ever leave the BFF. Zero Trust.
useCases.buyerStory: The agent must never hold or forward the user's raw access token — only scoped, exchanged agent tokens may leave the BFF.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The BFF performs RFC 8693 token exchange and enforces ff_skip_token_exchange fail-closed: an attempt to resolve a tool token by raw user-token forwarding is blocked with 403 user_token_forwarding_disabled at the source.
useCases.whatLong: An agent attempts to call an MCP tool by presenting the user's raw access token directly — no RFC 8693 exchange, no act claim, no scope narrowing. The BFF is the sole browser-token custodian and enforces the custody rule fail-closed: ff_skip_token_exchange arms the deny path, and agentMcpTokenService blocks the resolution with 403 user_token_forwarding_disabled before any gateway or Authorize call is made. The sim self-arms the flag, runs the real production resolver, and restores the prior flag value afterward.
useCases.businessValue: Token custody is enforced at the source, not downstream. The user token never crosses a process boundary to the agent runtime, the gateway, or the LLM context — eliminating confused-deputy and token-theft exposure at the widest attack surface: the agent itself.

productRoles.idp: Issues the user access token the agent attempts to forward.
productRoles.gw: Never reached on this path — the block fires at the BFF source, which is the demonstration point.

useCases.explicitTitle: Raw token forwarding blocked: passing a user token through an agent fails Zero Trust
useCases.valueStatement: Agents can't reuse your login token as their own: each hop must re-delegate properly, so a hijacked agent can't pose as your browser.

useCases.title: JIT / ephemeral credentials
useCases.oneLiner: The delegated token expires in minutes — a credential captured later is already dead.
useCases.buyerStory: A long-lived agent credential is a standing risk — tokens should be short-lived so a captured one is dead within minutes.
useCases.pingOneSolution: PingOne issues delegated tokens with a tight TTL; a refresh loop ensures the agent always holds a fresh credential.
useCases.whatLong: Long-lived agent credentials are a standing risk: a credential captured today is still valid tomorrow. This scenario demonstrates just-in-time ephemeral token issuance with short TTLs — a captured token expires in minutes, not days.
useCases.businessValue: Short-lived credentials are a built-in risk reducer. PingOne's token TTL configuration is the only control needed — no custom secret rotation infrastructure required.

productRoles.idp: Issues delegated tokens with a configurable TTL; the short expiry is enforced at introspection.
productRoles.gw: Introspects every token; a token past its TTL is rejected with 401 even if its signature is valid.

useCases.explicitTitle: Ephemeral credentials: delegated tokens expire in minutes
useCases.valueStatement: The theft window is minutes, not months: a captured agent token is already dead by the time an attacker tries it — no revocation scramble needed.

useCases.title: Rate-limit / resource-overload defense
useCases.oneLiner: Burst of tool calls → gateway returns 429 and cuts off the flood.
useCases.buyerStory: An agent flooding the gateway with tool calls must be throttled before it exhausts resources or runs up cost.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The agent gateway enforces per-agent / per-tool rate limits; a burst of calls is rejected with 429.
useCases.whatLong: An agent floods the gateway with rapid sequential tool calls — either to exhaust resources, rack up costs, or probe policy thresholds. The gateway enforces per-agent and per-tool rate limits; calls beyond the quota are rejected with 429 before any tool is dispatched.
useCases.businessValue: Rate limiting at the gateway perimeter protects upstream services and LLM budgets from runaway or adversarial agents — without application-layer changes.

productRoles.gw: Enforces per-agent / per-tool rate limits; returns 429 on quota breach before any tool dispatch.

useCases.explicitTitle: Flood defense: a burst of agent calls hits the 429 rate limit
useCases.valueStatement: A runaway or malicious agent can't take the service down for everyone: the gateway cuts off the flood while normal customers keep working.

useCases.title: Token-validation outage — fail closed
useCases.oneLiner: Kill token validation and the gateway stops every call cold — it never fails open.
useCases.buyerStory: If the token-validation backend itself goes down, the gateway must reject every call — not silently let traffic through.
useCases.pingOneSolution: Token validation is on the request path for every call; when it cannot be reached, the gateway fails closed rather than open.
useCases.whatLong: The gateway verifies the signature on every inbound token against the token issuer's JWKS (and introspects where introspection applies) before anything else runs. This scenario simulates that validation backend going unreachable and shows the gateway reject the call with a fail-closed 503, rather than letting it through.
useCases.businessValue: Many systems degrade to "allow" when their auth backend is unreachable. This gateway is built to fail closed instead — an outage in token validation becomes a blocked request, not an open door.

productRoles.gw: Verifies every token (JWKS signature; RFC 7662 introspection where configured) before evaluating policy; on validation failure, rejects the call with a 503 rather than forwarding it.

useCases.explicitTitle: Fail closed: when token validation is down, everything stops
useCases.valueStatement: An outage degrades to 'deny' not 'allow': attackers can't use an infrastructure failure as an open door, at the cost of brief unavailability.

useCases.title: Third-party MCP server, scoped at the gateway
useCases.oneLiner: Austin is in Texas — the gateway lets the call through to the real weather server.
useCases.buyerStory: A third-party tool the agent calls must be constrained to the business's actual footprint — even though the tool itself has no idea what that footprint is. That footprint should be something the business can change, not a hardcoded assumption.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The Agent Gateway fronts a third-party weather MCP server and enforces a live, admin-configurable state-scope policy (Texas by default) entirely at the edge — the backend never sees the restriction.
useCases.whatLong: The agent calls a real, unmodified third-party weather MCP server through the Agent Gateway. A city in the gateway's currently-configured state (Texas by default) is in scope for this demo policy, so the gateway forwards the call and the backend responds normally — the third-party server itself has no concept of the restriction.
useCases.businessValue: Any third-party or unmanaged MCP server can be brought into a governed environment without modifying it — the gateway enforces the business boundary, not the tool.

productRoles.gw: Validates the token, then runs the currently-configured state-scope policy (Texas by default) before forwarding the call to the third-party server.

useCases.explicitTitle: Third-party MCP server: scoped access at the gateway for external tools
useCases.valueStatement: You can adopt external tool servers without surrendering control: the gateway scopes what external tools may see and do.

useCases.title: Third-party MCP server — out-of-scope call denied
useCases.oneLiner: Miami is outside Texas — the gateway denies the call before the third-party server ever sees it.
useCases.buyerStory: When an agent's tool call falls outside the business's actual footprint, it must be stopped before the third-party tool ever runs — not after.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The Agent Gateway denies the call before it reaches the third-party weather MCP server, based on the currently-configured state scope (Texas by default) — the demo policy the backend never sees.
useCases.whatLong: The agent asks for weather in a city outside the demo policy's currently-configured state scope (Texas by default). The gateway denies the call before it is ever forwarded to the third-party weather MCP server — the backend never runs, and never sees the request.
useCases.businessValue: Scoping happens once, at the gateway, instead of being re-implemented (or forgotten) in every tool integration — a policy change takes effect for every agent immediately.

productRoles.gw: Runs the currently-configured state-scope policy (Texas by default) and returns DENY before the call is forwarded to the third-party server.

useCases.explicitTitle: Third-party MCP: an out-of-scope call to an external server is denied
useCases.valueStatement: External integrations obey the same rules as internal ones: the scope grant is the boundary, enforced at the gateway every call.

useCases.title: Live-reconfigure the gateway's scope policy
useCases.oneLiner: Watch: the same "weather in Miami" query — denied under Texas, permitted the moment I switch this dropdown to Any.
useCases.buyerStory: A demo of a policy control isn't credible if the policy is actually hardcoded in the app. The business needs to change the rule itself — live, without a code change or a restart — and see the SAME request's outcome flip.
useCases.pingOneSolution: An admin-editable Allowed State control, right on the gateway capability card, changes ff_weather_mcp_allowed_state live; the Agent Gateway reads it on the very next request, no restart.
useCases.whatLong: UC30/UC31 each show one fixed outcome (Texas permits Austin, denies Miami). This use case is the proof that the scope itself is a live, admin-owned policy value — not app logic: switch the Allowed State dropdown on the Weather MCP page to Michigan, Any, or back to Texas, and the exact same weather chat query changes its outcome immediately, with no gateway restart. Leaving the page restores Texas, so the next pass of UC30/UC31 starts from the documented policy.
useCases.businessValue: A policy that can only be changed by redeploying code isn't really externalized governance — it just moved the hardcoding one layer down. Making the scope itself admin-editable, live, is what makes the "the gateway decides, not the app" story provable in front of a customer.

productRoles.gw: Reads the currently-configured state on every request via the same flag-check call that already gates ff_weather_mcp_showcase — no new round-trip.

useCases.explicitTitle: Live policy edit: tighten the gateway scope list and the next call moves
useCases.valueStatement: Policy changes take effect on the next call, not the next deploy: security teams respond to incidents in seconds.

useCases.title: Third-party search server, filtered at the gateway
useCases.oneLiner: An ordinary business search — no blocked term, so the gateway forwards it to the real Brave API.
useCases.buyerStory: An agent that can search the open web is useful and dangerous in the same breath. The business needs the useful half without hand-auditing every query, and without asking the search vendor to enforce a policy it has never heard of.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The Agent Gateway fronts a third-party Brave Search MCP server and inspects the query argument against a content policy before the request leaves the perimeter — the search vendor never sees a blocked query at all.
useCases.whatLong: The agent calls a real, unmodified third-party MCP server fronting the Brave Search API. The query carries no blocked term, so the Agent Gateway forwards it and the live search result comes back — the third-party server itself has no concept of the bank's content policy.
useCases.businessValue: Egress control on tool calls: an unmanaged third-party search server can be brought inside a governed perimeter without modifying it or trusting it.

productRoles.gw: Validates the token, runs the content-blocklist policy against the query argument, then forwards the call to the third-party server.

useCases.explicitTitle: Third-party search filtered: results scoped before they reach the agent
useCases.valueStatement: External search results are filtered at the gateway, so a third party can't leak data into your agent's context.

useCases.title: Third-party search server — blocked query denied
useCases.oneLiner: Demo bank policy says no crypto research through the agent gateway. The gateway kills the query before Brave ever sees it.
useCases.buyerStory: A policy that only catches bad queries after the vendor has already run them is not a control. The block has to happen before the request leaves the building.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The Agent Gateway denies the call at the edge when the query contains a blocked term, so the request is never sent to Brave — no vendor log, no billed call, no data leaving the perimeter.
useCases.whatLong: The agent is asked to search for a term on the demo bank's content blocklist (bitcoin / cryptocurrency / crypto). The Agent Gateway matches the term in the query argument and returns DENY before the call is forwarded — the third-party Brave server never runs the search and never sees the query.
useCases.businessValue: Data-egress control sits in one place at the gateway instead of being re-implemented, or forgotten, in every tool integration.

productRoles.gw: Runs the content-blocklist policy against the query argument and returns DENY before the call is forwarded to the third-party server.

useCases.explicitTitle: Third-party search blocked: a query outside the grant is denied
useCases.valueStatement: The grant defines the queries: external providers can't expand what they answer beyond what was permitted.

useCases.title: Protected RAG
useCases.oneLiner: The answer is grounded in indexed code, but retrieval happens only after RFC 8693 delegation, code:search scope enforcement, and a PingOne Authorize PERMIT.
useCases.buyerStory: Grounded code retrieval is useful only when the agent cannot widen its own access to the indexed source.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The BFF exchanges the user token for a delegated MCP token with code:search, then the Agent Gateway and PingOne Authorize enforce the code_search call before Weaviate retrieval.
useCases.whatLong: The chip routes deterministically to code_search. useCases.title: Consumer Agent — governed flight booking
useCases.oneLiner: The agent found the flight and proposed the booking — but the price had to pass the transaction policy, and the booking only ran after you approved it. Then "show my reservations" shows the trip it booked.
useCases.buyerStory: A consumer agent asked to "book me a flight to Paris under $800" must prove who it acts for, accept the price policy, and pause for the human when the transaction is consequential.
useCases.pingOneSolution: The agent exchanges the user token (RFC 8693), PingOne Authorize evaluates the booking price against the transaction policy, returns a HITL consent obligation, and only a verified human approval receipt lets the booking write reach the reservations database.
useCases.whatLong: A consumer agent is asked to book a flight from San Francisco to Paris for two passengers, under $800. The site detects the agent, the user signs in, and the agent exchanges the user authority for a delegated token with an act claim. The booking price ($346) is evaluated against the transaction policy: a HITL consent obligation comes back, the agent pauses and surfaces a consent modal, and only the human approval receipt — verified, bound to this user, agent, and tool — discharges the gate. The retry PERMITs and the booking write lands in the reservations database, where the ordinary "show my reservations" read lists it. Passkey registration and agent-permission preferences (Co-Pilot/Auto-Pilot/Read-only) are the trust setup that precedes this governed run.
useCases.businessValue: Consumer agents can complete high-street transactions without losing human control: the price policy and consent receipt make the booking auditable end to end, and the agent cannot bypass the pause no matter how it phrases the request.
